items.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Dizzy’s a marvelous trumpet player, but Miles is a poet.

ctx.x: They were trained to listen to music. We have audiences that go into concert halls. They’re trained to listen to music. They don’t applaud until the piece is over. I argued with many bandleaders. I used to say to Woody [Herman], “Why do you say, ‘Joe Yivta on trombone, ladies and gentlemen,’ while so-and-so is playing, taking the lead and doing something. You’re wasting his whole . . .” “Well, the audience likes it.” I said, “But what do you like, Woody? Don’t you think it’s time you told them, ‘Wait until after…

I’d say, “For Christ’s sake, if you guys aren’t listening to him, what do you expect the audience to do? They’re listening with their eyes. Show some respect for this guy.” They got that. “I can dig it. I can dig it.” From there on in, they understood that music is also watched. You’re playing for an audience. It’s very hard to make the average musician understand that if you want any dignity for the music, you’ve got to give it some. It’s one of the things I liked about Miles [Davis].
